meta.title: Interim Impact Evaluation of the Agri-Tech Catalyst: Phase 1 - Final Report
meta.topic: Collaborative agricultural technology research, development and commercialisation

brief.intended_change: Accelerate translation of research into practical agricultural solutions and encourage greater R&D, ultimately supporting UK economic growth and agricultural productivity while improving animal welfare and reducing environmental impacts.
brief.population: UK agri-tech businesses, including SMEs, and research organisations participating in collaborative R&D; ultimately the wider agricultural sector.
brief.time_horizon: Programme delivery shown as 2014–2017, with anticipated outputs in 2015–2020 and outcomes and impacts in 2016–2025. Phase 1 evaluation research took place between February and June 2018.
brief.intervention: The Agri-Tech Catalyst provides competitive grants for collaborative industry–research projects at early, industrial research and late stages of development. The programme description identifies £60 million of non-DFID grant funding, alongside operational delivery and strategic oversight. This evaluation phase covers early and late stage awards only; project-specific grant amounts and durations are not supplied in the extracts.
brief.context: The programme forms part of the UK Agri-Tech Strategy. Its rationale includes risky R&D, uncertain and delayed returns, coordination problems, information failures and spillovers. Most surveyed applicants were already R&D-active. DFID-funded projects are outside this evaluation's scope.
brief.outcome_first: Develop a theory of change for accelerating the translation of research into practical agricultural solutions in the United Kingdom. It should address UK agri-tech businesses and research organisations, with longer-term ambitions for economic growth, agricultural productivity, animal welfare and environmental sustainability.
brief.intervention_first: Develop a theory of change for the UK Agri-Tech Catalyst's competitive grants for collaborative industry–research R&D projects. Explain how the programme could accelerate practical agricultural innovation and contribute to business growth, agricultural productivity, animal welfare and environmental sustainability.

overall.raw: Early evidence gathered for this first phase of the evaluation suggests the programme is performing well against its aims to “accelerate translation of research into practical solutions, best practices …” and encourage greater R&D in the sector. It is probably too early to assess whether this is then translating into “… applications of new technologies in agriculture”, increased turnover and exports, improved agricultural productivity and reducing environmental impacts, and improved competitive position of the UK’s agri-tech sector internationally.
overall.quote: performing well ... It is probably too early to assess

conclusions.summary: The intended pathway was judged plausible and the rationale strongly supported by risk, uncertain and delayed returns, and coordination failures, although evidence of finance constraints was mixed. Early and late stage projects show strong technological, skills, capacity and collaboration benefits, including sustained behavioural changes. Some products have reached market and some firms have substantial revenues, but aggregate commercial and wider agricultural impacts remain modest or prospective. ATC is an important and sometimes decisive contributor, especially to intermediate outcomes, while further investments and activity are generally needed to realise commercial and economic potential. The assessment covers only early and late stage awards, approximately half the portfolio, and relies substantially on triangulated self-reported evidence rather than a statistical counterfactual.
recommendations: Probe how and why projects require external innovation support outside their consortia in the next evaluation phase.
Give greater attention to dissemination, knowledge exchange and the mechanisms by which project benefits will spread to the wider agricultural sector.
Address the identified gaps in awareness of and access to follow-on private finance.
The report states that a comprehensive programme assessment and recommendations for a final impact evaluation will follow in Phase 2.

open_questions: Figure 8-2 on p106 is transcribed as the populated version of Figure 3-3 on p33. The programme logic model on p32 and progress summary on p102 are not transcribed as separate diagrams.

The small image makes several shared arrow junctions difficult to resolve. In particular, verify the grant-type-to-output junctions, the reciprocal technological-progress/follow-on-investment connection, the inputs to the new/strengthened relationships box, and the lower branches feeding future impacts against a higher-resolution original. No uncertain additional inputs to the relationships box have been invented.
Future expected impacts are indicated by dashed box outlines in Figure 8-2; the record has no separate field for that graphical distinction.

Figure 8-2's legend distinguishes intermediate outcomes from final outcomes/impacts. Intermediate outcomes are mapped to outcome_short and final outcomes/impacts to impact; the source does not separately divide short- and long-term outcomes.

The p102 tick scale measures progress, not evidence of causal effect. Strong progress is mapped to supports; some and limited progress are mapped to partly, preserving the original wording. These verdicts are attached to results, not to every connecting arrow.

The p102 progress items do not always exactly match the broader composite boxes in Figure 8-2. In particular, 'Greater understanding of innovation processes' is narrower than b15. Composite verdicts should not be read as evidence for every clause.

Figure 8-1 gives three ticks for additional private investment, patents, collaborations, skills and commercial applications; two for research outputs and new data. The differing output findings are retained in k4 rather than represented as invented individual boxes.

Figure 8-1 gives two ticks for university attitudes/behaviour, while the text also describes sustained changes in both university and business behaviour. These are different scopes, not necessarily contradictory verdicts.
The original p33 diagram includes a developing-country food-security/poverty impact. It is absent from the populated p106 diagram; DFID-funded projects are explicitly outside this evaluation's scope.
The provided text reports 74% fully additional outcomes on p85, while Figure 7-1's rounded categories on p86 sum to 76%. Both are source values; they have not been reconciled.

The p140 case study corroborates k3, k7 and k8: complementary partners enabled a larger, quicker and better-quality project; specific skills were directly attributable to ATC, while feeder projects, equipment and institutional changes also contributed.
Recommendations concerning finance and knowledge exchange reflect explicit gaps identified in the supplied findings and Figure 8-2, rather than a supplied formal recommendations section.

The supplied extracts do not establish publication metadata, URLs or licence. The year 2018 follows the evaluation timing; verify it against the report cover. Evidence level B is a provisional classification for the mixed-methods contribution analysis because no A/B/C rubric was supplied.
No separate causal studies are named for the programme steps. Methodological references and the Smart programme comparator are not treated as studies establishing individual ATC causal links.
Phase 2 was not supplied and its findings are not incorporated.
